description: We are some enthusiastic people interested in technology, Earth science, or research. What matters most is curiosity, commitment, creativity, and a genuine interest in building something meaningful together.
summary:
SPACESAGE turns the Earth into sound. Our web app takes NASA Earth Information Center pictures and plays each one as music: the picture is read from left to right in 48 time slices, and warmer colours raise the pitch, brightness sets the loudness, and sharp edges add a tick. Six climate stories, from wildfires and cyclones to sea ice and greenhouse gases, each has its own voice, and visitors can upload any picture of their own. Story mode plays all six in turn with captions, and every melody can be exported as a WAV file. Uploaded pictures never leave the visitor's device.

The challenge asks us to make Earth science accessible through sound. SPACESAGE does that by design: every picture has a written description and a summary of its melody, so blind and low-vision listeners can follow the same data as everyone else.

The WHO estimates at least 2.2 billion people have a vision impairment or blindness, and Bangladesh faces serious air pollution and cyclone risks. SPACESAGE shows that Earth's changing story can be heard as well as seen.
details:
SPACESAGE – The Earth Jukebox

What it does:
SPACESAGE turns NASA Earth Information Center pictures into music. A visitor chooses one of six climate topics (wildfires, air quality, temperature, sea ice, cyclones and greenhouse gases), or uploads their own picture, presses play, and hears the picture read from left to right as a melody. A signal view shows the three sound layers moving with the sound. Story mode plays all six topics in turn with a caption for each, and any melody can be exported as a WAV sound file. Every picture also has a written description and a short summary of where the melody goes, so the experience works with or without sound.

How it works:
Each picture is cut into 48 time slices, read left to right. Every slice is split into three horizontal bands: top, middle and bottom. In each band we measure warmth (red minus blue) and brightness; in the whole slice we measure contrast. The middle band sets the lead melody, where warmer means higher. The bottom band sets a deep bass line, and the top band sets a high shimmer. Brightness sets loudness, and sharp contrast adds a short tick. Each topic has its own voice, with its own scale of five to seven notes, instrument, rhythm and tick sound, so fire crackles, ice rings like glass and storms swirl. Playback uses a lookahead scheduler, so the timing stays steady even when the page is busy. The same analysis runs in the browser and in Python, and the two agree to within a rounding error of about one part in ten trillion.

Benefits and intended impact:
Most Earth science reaches the public as pictures, and sight-only data leaves many people out. The World Health Organization estimates that at least 2.2 billion people have a vision impairment or blindness. SPACESAGE gives them, and anyone who prefers listening, a way into the same data. In Bangladesh, the World Bank estimates 78,145 to 88,229 deaths from air pollution in 2019, and puts Dhaka's yearly average fine-particle level at 90 to 100 µg/m³. Storm risk is real as well: the 1970 Bhola cyclone is the deadliest tropical cyclone on record. We hope the melody makes a trend, such as a fire season or a warming year, easier to feel and remember, and that the same method could sit beside any NASA Earth visual.

Tools, languages, hardware and software:
Languages: HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Python. Browser technologies: the Web Audio API (live synthesis and offline rendering to WAV), the Canvas API (picture analysis and the signal view), the Speech Synthesis API (spoken description, where the browser supports it) and the Vibration API (Android only). Python libraries: Pillow and NumPy, used to make the pre-made audio and data files. Testing: Node.js, with 21 automated checks run against a simulated audio clock. Hosting: Netlify, with security headers. Hardware: no special hardware; any phone or computer with a modern browser. The site uses no external libraries and no server, and uploaded pictures never leave the visitor's device.


The project treats data as music rather than as a chart. Each topic has its own sound identity. Story mode turns six climate facts into a short listening journey, and the signal view lets sighted viewers see the mapping while they hear it. The logo follows the same idea: a globe, a waveform and an orbit.

Factors the team considered:
Accessibility: every picture has a text description and a melody summary, the site works with the keyboard and screen readers, and it respects the reduced-motion setting. Scientific honesty: colour is treated as a proxy, and the limits are stated on the site. For example, on maps the left-to-right scan follows geography rather than time, so the melody changes less. Privacy: no accounts, no tracking and no uploads. Speed: the first screen is about 28 KB, and pictures and audio load only when they are chosen. Reproducibility: the mapping is deterministic, so the same picture always gives the same melody.


A transparent, stated mapping, with a check that a flipped picture changes 48 of 48 slices in the bass and shimmer layers.
Best Use of Data: NASA Earth Information Center and NASA Scientific Visualization Studio pictures made audible, with sources and credits listed.
Lookahead audio scheduling, offline WAV rendering in the browser, and a Python pipeline that produces matching audio and data files.
Art and Technology: one voice per topic, and a visual identity that matches the sound.
Best Use of Storytelling: a six-part story mode with captions, and descriptions that can be read aloud.
Letting people hear the planet change.
Best Mission Concept: a lightweight, open-source sound layer that could sit beside any Earth Information Center visual. This is a proposal and has not been built into NASA's site.
Built around Bangladesh's air pollution and cyclone risk.
Galactic Impact: a free, open web tool that makes Earth science more accessible to people everywhere.
